lead: Real gases do not obey pv = RT exactly. The compressibility factor Z = pv/RT measures the correction: Z is 1 for an ideal gas and moves away from 1 near the critical point and at high pressure. Engineers read Z from a generalized chart using reduced pressure and temperature, then get v = ZRT/p. This matters for filling a CNG cylinder at 200 bar, sizing gas pipelines, and checking when the ideal-gas answer is safe.
prereq: You need: 5.7 ideal and real gases and 5.2 critical properties.

blocks.text: A real gas approaches ideal behaviour only at low pressure and high temperature. The compressibility factor Z measures the gap. At a given pressure and temperature, Z = pv/(RT). At the same p and T, an ideal gas has v<sub>ideal</sub> = RT/p, so Z = v<sub>actual</sub>/v<sub>ideal</sub>. For an ideal gas, Z = 1. For steam near saturation, Z can be well below 1. For nitrogen at ordinary conditions, Z is close to 1.

blocks.where: p is absolute pressure in Pa or kPa; v is specific volume in m³/kg; R is the gas constant in J/(kg·K) or kJ/(kg·K); T is absolute temperature in kelvin; v<sub>ideal</sub> = RT/p.

blocks.text: To compare gases, scale by critical properties: pR = p/pc, TR = T/Tc, and vR = v/vc. Here pc and Tc are the critical pressure and temperature from 5.2, and vc is the critical specific volume. These ratios are dimensionless. Some charts use pseudoreduced volume vR′ = v/(RTc/pc) instead. The principle of corresponding states says gases with the same pR and TR have approximately the same Z. That is why one chart works for many gases. Some syllabi call it the generalized compressibility chart.

Written with v<sub>R</sub> = v/v<sub>c</sub>, the van der Waals equation of 5.7 loses its constants: (p<sub>R</sub> + 3/v<sub>R</sub>²)(3v<sub>R</sub> − 1) = 8T<sub>R</sub>. This reduced equation of state is the simplest argument for corresponding states. It also predicts the same critical compressibility Z<sub>c</sub> = p<sub>c</sub>v<sub>c</sub>/(RT<sub>c</sub>) = 0.375 for every gas; measured values are lower, about 0.29 for nitrogen and methane, 0.27 for carbon dioxide and 0.23 for water, which is why charts built from data beat the reduced van der Waals equation.

The chart plots p<sub>R</sub> on the horizontal axis and Z on the vertical axis. Curves are lines of constant T<sub>R</sub>. At very low p<sub>R</sub>, every curve meets Z = 1: the gas is ideal. At high p<sub>R</sub>, the curves spread apart. Near T<sub>R</sub> = 1 the curve dips sharply to low Z because attractive forces are strong close to the critical point. For T<sub>R</sub> below 1 the dip ends where the saturation line cuts the curve. At high T<sub>R</sub>, Z stays near 1 or rises above 1 as pressure grows. The chart is approximate; read Z to two or three significant figures.

items: Find p<sub>c</sub> and T<sub>c</sub> for the gas.
Use absolute pressure and kelvin temperature.
Compute p<sub>R</sub> = p/p<sub>c</sub> and T<sub>R</sub> = T/T<sub>c</sub>.
Locate the point on the chart and read Z; interpolate between T<sub>R</sub> curves if needed.
Compute v = ZRT/p with matching units.

blocks.text: Do not use gauge pressure or Celsius in pR and TR. The chart does not need the gas identity beyond pc and Tc, but it is less accurate for polar gases such as water and ammonia. For those, use tables or a suitable equation of state. Mixtures need pseudocritical properties (Kay’s rule, in 5.9).

Once Z is known, v = ZRT/p. Use p in kPa with R in kJ/(kg·K), because 1 kJ = 1 kPa·m³. For total volume, V = m v. The same correction appears as pV = mZRT. If Z > 1, the gas is less compressible than ideal (it occupies more volume, repulsive forces dominate). If Z < 1, it is more compressible than ideal (it occupies less volume, attractive forces dominate). At low p<sub>R</sub> or high T<sub>R</sub>, the ideal-gas answer is close. At p<sub>R</sub> near 1 and T<sub>R</sub> near 1, the ideal-gas law can be badly wrong.

blocks.where: v is specific volume in m³/kg; Z is the compressibility factor from the chart; R is the gas constant in kJ/(kg·K); T is kelvin; p is absolute pressure in kPa.

blocks.text: The chart is a hand tool for quick estimates. Detailed process design uses cubic equations of state or reference databases, as noted in 5.7. The worked examples apply the chart route to a CNG cylinder, where Z is well below 1, and to nitrogen, where it is close to 1.

examples.question: A CNG cylinder of internal volume 60 litres is filled with methane to 20 MPa at 300 K. For methane T<sub>c</sub> = 190.6 K, p<sub>c</sub> = 4.60 MPa and R = 0.5183 kJ/(kg·K). Estimate the mass of gas (a) with the ideal gas law, (b) with Z from the generalized compressibility chart.
steps: Reduced temperature: T<sub>R</sub> = 300/190.6 = 1.574. Reduced pressure: p<sub>R</sub> = 20/4.60 = 4.35.
Chart: at T<sub>R</sub> ≈ 1.57 and p<sub>R</sub> ≈ 4.35 the chart gives Z ≈ 0.83 (Figure 5.8.1).
The ideal law underestimates the fill by 9.30 − 7.72 = 1.58 kg, about 17 per cent. Reference data for methane give Z = 0.828 and 9.32 kg, so the chart is within 0.3 per cent.
examples.answer: T<sub>R</sub> = 1.57, p<sub>R</sub> = 4.35, Z ≈ 0.83; the cylinder holds about 9.3 kg of methane, not the 7.7 kg the ideal law predicts.

examples.question: Nitrogen is stored at 300 K and 10 MPa. For nitrogen p<sub>c</sub> = 3.39 MPa, T<sub>c</sub> = 126.2 K, R = 0.2968 kJ/(kg·K). Find T<sub>R</sub>, p<sub>R</sub>, and estimate the specific volume v using Z from the generalized chart.
steps: On the chart the T<sub>R</sub> = 2.4 curve sits almost exactly on Z = 1 at p<sub>R</sub> ≈ 3: read Z ≈ 1.00.
Reference data give Z = 1.005 here, so the ideal-gas answer is good to about half a per cent: at this high T<sub>R</sub> the attraction and the molecular volume nearly cancel.

traps: Using gauge pressure in p<sub>R</sub>. p<sub>R</sub> needs absolute pressure; a gauge reading of 9.9 MPa at 0.1 MPa atmosphere is 10 MPa absolute.
Using Celsius in T<sub>R</sub>. All reduced temperatures use kelvin.
Taking p<sub>c</sub> and T<sub>c</sub> for air when the gas is nitrogen, oxygen or carbon dioxide.
Using v = RT/p when the chart shows Z far from 1, such as near the critical point.
Mixing units: R in kJ/(kg·K) requires p in kPa, not MPa.

quiz.a: Z = pv/(RT), where p is absolute pressure, v is specific volume, R is the gas constant and T is kelvin; Z compares actual volume with ideal volume at the same p and T.

quiz.q: Write the definitions of p<sub>R</sub> and T<sub>R</sub>.
quiz.a: p<sub>R</sub> = p/p<sub>c</sub> and T<sub>R</sub> = T/T<sub>c</sub>, with p<sub>c</sub> and T<sub>c</sub> the critical pressure and temperature.

quiz.q: Why can one compressibility chart be used for many different gases?
quiz.a: The principle of corresponding states says gases at the same reduced pressure and reduced temperature have approximately the same Z. Critical properties absorb the differences between gases, so one chart works approximately for many gases.

quiz.q: What does Z < 1 mean for a real gas?
quiz.a: At the same pressure and temperature, the real gas occupies less volume than an ideal gas. It is more compressible than ideal because attractive forces pull molecules closer.

quiz.q: Carbon dioxide has p<sub>c</sub> = 7.38 MPa and T<sub>c</sub> = 304.1 K. Find p<sub>R</sub> and T<sub>R</sub> at 5 MPa and 300 K.
quiz.a: p<sub>R</sub> = 5/7.38 = 0.678. T<sub>R</sub> = 300/304.1 = 0.987. Both are near 1, so the gas is close to its critical region and Z is far from 1 (about 0.69).

quiz.q: The CNG cylinder of the worked example is filled only to 10 MPa at 300 K, where the chart gives Z ≈ 0.86. How much methane does it hold?
A gas state has p<sub>R</sub> = 3, T<sub>R</sub> = 1.1 and Z = 0.7. Does the ideal-gas law overpredict or underpredict the volume, and by what percentage?
quiz.a: Actual v = 0.7 RT/p, so ideal v<sub>ideal</sub> = RT/p is larger. The ideal-gas law overpredicts by (1/0.7 − 1) × 100 ≈ 43%.

quiz.q: Why is the simple compressibility chart less accurate for steam near saturation?
quiz.a: Steam is polar and hydrogen-bonded, so its molecules do not follow the simple corresponding-states behaviour. The chart assumes non-polar behaviour and works best for simple gases; steam needs steam tables or a better equation of state.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, compressibility factors feed into pipeline hydraulics for natural gas and into LNG storage calculations. Process simulators use equations of state such as Peng-Robinson or Lee-Kesler instead of a hand chart. Research on corresponding states extends the idea to mixtures and polar fluids. Search for the principle of corresponding states, the Lee-Kesler chart, and NIST REFPROP.
